description: We’re a team of 5 Computer Science students and software developers (front end, data/algorithms, and interactive/game dev). Our team is already complete, so we’re not recruiting right now. We’re exploring a web tool to compare lunar south pole landing sites by Sun and Earth visibility, and our idea may still evolve. Good luck to all participants!
summary:
ViaLunae is a web-based lunar surface simulator that helps mission planners compare landing and operation sites by sunlight, terrain and solar power. The user picks a location, a start time and a duration. The tool computes sunlight over time using the real terrain horizon up to 150 km and estimates, in kW, the output of a solar panel the user configures: area, efficiency and orientation. Scenarios can be added to a comparison table, sorted by any column and exported as CSV. The interface is available in Portuguese and English.

Lunar missions have been cut short by power, communication, illumination and landing-site constraints; for example, IM-2 Athena operated about 12 of its 240 planned hours. ViaLunae does not predict landing failures: it supports the evaluation of operating conditions at a given site and date before a mission. It uses NASA Moon Trek imagery.
details:
1. DETAILED PROJECT DESCRIPTION

WHY VIALUNAE EXISTS

The lunar south pole is the hardest place to land and the most wanted: the Sun skims the horizon, crater floors stay in shadow, and the Earth sits low in the sky and can drop out of view. Recent landers show how little margin there is:

  • SLIM (JAXA, Jan 2024): lost an engine on descent and landed nose-down with its solar panels facing west. It shut down about 3 hours after landing with 12% battery, and recovered days later when the Sun direction changed.
  • IM-1 Odysseus (Intuitive Machines, Feb 2024): caught a foot on the surface and tipped over onto a rock, which made it hard to point its antennas at the Earth. It operated about 6 days against about a week planned.
  • IM-2 Athena (Intuitive Machines, Mar 2025): landed on its side inside a crater near Mons Mouton, roughly 250 m from target by the company's figure and more than 400 m by NASA's. It operated about 12 h 45 min against 10 days planned.
  • VIPER (NASA, not flown): designed to survive at most about 50 hours of darkness, and at the pole the Earth can be out of sight for about two weeks of every month.

In the three flights, the trigger was landing and attitude, and the consequence was power and communication. Planning tools exist, but 3D line-of-sight analysis lives in specialist software, while the public maps (QuickMap, Moon Trek) are 2D. ViaLunae puts site, date, horizon, power and communication in one page that anyone can open.

WHAT VIALUNAE DOES

  • 3D globe of the Moon (CesiumJS) with the south pole view, fixed sites (six Apollo sites, Mons Mouton and Malapert A) and free coordinates by typing or clicking.
  • Sun and Earth on the real horizon: azimuth and elevation of both for any date, with the terrain profile deciding what is visible.
  • Metrics per scenario: sunlight percentage and longest lit period, time to next sunset or sunrise, Earth-visible windows and signal delay, solar power in kW and energy in kWh, ground irradiance, estimated surface temperature.
  • Conditions at the site at any instant of a timeline, with animation and speed control, plus charts of Sun/Earth elevation, irradiance and temperature.
  • Ground view: a camera 2 m above the surface with real relief, with the Sun and Earth placed in the sky by the timeline.
  • Comparison table for up to 12 scenarios: sort by any column, best value highlighted in green, CSV export.
  • PT/EN interface and a public codebase with automated tests.

Figure 1: globe at the south pole with Mons Mouton selected and the scenario results panel (14 Nov 2026, 30 days, panel set to 12.6 m², relief on).

Figure 2: "Conditions at the site" card with the horizon panorama (relief in grey, Sun and Earth paths), the Sun and Earth elevation chart, and the irradiance and temperature chart.

HOW IT WORKS: KEY TECHNICAL DECISIONS

  • Ephemerides, not approximations. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441). The browser cannot call Horizons directly (no CORS), so two serverless functions on Vercel act as a validated, cached proxy. Fixed sites ship with 12 months of hourly data pre-computed (1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2027); any other site or period is fetched live.
  • A real horizon up to 150 km. The pole's light depends on mountains tens of kilometres away, so a smooth-sphere horizon is wrong. For each site the app samples the Cesium Moon terrain (NASA and USGS data) in 180 directions and 27 distances out to 150 km, in two passes (near and far), and builds a horizon profile. The Sun or the Earth only counts as visible above that profile. Fixed sites have the profile pre-computed; free coordinates are computed in the browser (about 30 to 70 seconds) and cached.
  • Power model. Irradiance is 1361 W/m² divided by the squared Sun distance (from Horizons), times the cosine of the incidence angle on the panel. Three panel modes: vertical rotating to follow the Sun (default), two-axis tracking, fixed tilt and azimuth. Area and efficiency are editable and the result recalculates instantly. Anything behind the relief produces zero.
  • Temperature model (estimate). Radiative equilibrium by day (albedo 0.12, emissivity 0.95) and a night floor by latitude. The screen says it is an estimate.
  • Comparison by design. Every metric is computed by pure functions shared by the screen, the table and the CSV, so the three cannot disagree. The suite has 21 automated tests (metrics, power, conditions, comparison).
  • Credits on every layer: NASA/JPL Horizons, Cesium Moon Terrain, LROC WAC imagery via NASA Moon Trek.

Figure 3: ground view, 2 m above Mons Mouton, looking at the Sun on 22 Nov 2026 at 02:00 UTC, with relief on the horizon.

2. CASE STUDY: REPLAYING IM-2 ATHENA'S SITE

We asked ViaLunae what the target site looked like during the 10 days Athena was planned to operate, starting 6 March 2025 at 17:00 UTC (approximately its landing time) at Mons Mouton (84.79 S, 29.20 E), with the real horizon on.

  • Sun above the terrain horizon: 100% of the 10 planned days.
  • Sun elevation: 2.4 to 5.4 degrees (mean 4.4).
  • Earth above the terrain horizon: 100% of the 10 planned days.

What it says. At the target coordinates, the Sun and the Earth were both above the horizon for the whole planned mission, so illumination and communication geometry at the site were not the limit. Sources report that Athena instead stopped after about 12 h 45 min after landing on its side inside a crater, with the Sun direction, the panel orientation and the cold preventing it from recharging. With the Sun only 2 to 5 degrees above the horizon, a few degrees of tilt or a crater wall around the real landing spot is enough to remove nearly all light.

What it does not say. The model sees a 150 km horizon at the target coordinates. It does not see crater-scale shadows 250 to 400 m away, where Athena actually stopped, nor the lander's tilt. That gap is the next feature on our roadmap, and it is why ViaLunae treats its result as "is this site worth considering", not "this landing will succeed".

3. COMPARING SITES AND DATES

The same engine, 30 days from 1 Nov 2026, default panel (10 m², 30% efficiency, vertical rotating):

  • Mons Mouton (IM-2 Athena): sun 59.2% on a smooth sphere and 53.3% with real relief; longest lit period 377 h; Earth visible 74.1% (smooth) and 88.9% (relief); mean power 2.20 kW; ground irradiance 58 W/m²; temperature -219 to -46 °C.
  • Malapert A (IM-1 Odysseus): sun 55.6% smooth and 47.9% with relief; longest lit period 316 h; Earth visible 100%; mean power 1.97 kW; ground irradiance 92 W/m²; temperature -215 to -14 °C.
  • Apollo 11 (equator): sun 49.4% smooth and 49.2% with relief; longest lit period 354 h; Earth visible 100%; mean power 1.31 kW; ground irradiance 436 W/m²; temperature -178 to 115 °C.

Three things this comparison shows that a smooth sphere hides:

  1. Relief changes the answer in both directions. At Mons Mouton the terrain takes sunlight from 59% to 53%, and at Malapert A from 56% to 48%, but it raises Earth visibility at Mons Mouton from 74% to 89%, because the massif sits above the surrounding ground and sees below the smooth-sphere horizon.
  2. The pole's mean power can beat the equator's while its light is much weaker. With a vertical panel that follows the Sun, a low Sun still lights the panel face-on, so mean power is higher at the pole than at Apollo 11 (2.20 versus 1.31 kW) even though ground irradiance is 58 versus 436 W/m². The temperature range shows the cost: the pole never warms past -14 °C.
  3. Over a full year the picture shifts. With relief on, sunlight falls to 44.7% (Mons Mouton) and 41.7% (Malapert A), against 48.6% at Apollo 11, and Earth visibility at Mons Mouton drops to 86.6%.

Figure 4: the comparison table with Mons Mouton, Malapert A and Apollo 11 loaded (panel set to 12.6 m² in this screenshot, so its kW and kWh are higher than the figures above).

How the numbers were produced. The figures above come from the project's own pre-computed ephemerides and horizon profiles (and, for March 2025, from the app's live /api/sky function), run through the same metrics, power and conditions code the app uses. They are model outputs, not flight telemetry.

4. LIMITS WE STATE ON PURPOSE

  • No validation against flight data yet. We replay Athena's site but we do not claim that the model predicts its outcome.
  • Horizon resolution: 2 degree steps in azimuth and terrain out to 150 km, with no crater-scale shadows and no lander tilt.
  • Temperature is an equilibrium estimate with a night floor by latitude, not a thermal simulation.
  • Panel model: no dust, degradation or self-shadowing by the lander.
  • Pre-computed window: fixed sites cover 1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2027. Other periods use the live API (up to 400 days).
  • 3D terrain uses a Cesium ion token.

5. ROADMAP

Done: globe, horizon, power, conditions, ground view, comparison, CSV, PT/EN, tests. Planned, not built yet:

  1. Educational mode: short "?" cards on each metric, a first-visit tour, and cards on why the pole is hard.
  2. Traffic-light filters per variable (solar energy, relief and shadow, Earth communication, available time). Each filter shows red, yellow or green, filters stack, and any can be switched off. Open design question we want to test with users: equal weights, user-set weights, or filters that can veto a site outright.
  3. Landing-risk parameters taken from what actually went wrong: panel orientation, tilt at landing, terrain slope, landing precision (distance from target), crater cold, night length, Earth visibility, and rocks near the pad.
  4. Crater-scale shadows from high-resolution LOLA relief around candidate sites, which would close the gap shown in the Athena case study.
  5. Replay mode for past missions so each failure can be loaded with the conditions it landed in.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS AND VISION

  • Treat the site and the date as one decision. The same coordinates give very different light and Earth contact on different weeks.
  • Plan with the real horizon, not a smooth sphere. Differences of several percentage points of sunlight, in either direction, are common (see section 3).
  • Design for tilt. Three recent landers ended up tilted or on their side. Power and antenna margins at a given tilt should be a standard input to site selection.
  • Share the same open data. Everything in ViaLunae comes from public NASA and USGS data, so a student team and a mission team can look at the same numbers.

Sources for the mission facts: SLIM, JAXA statements reported by AFP and Reuters; IM-1, AP and Gizmodo; IM-2, Intuitive Machines and NASA as reported by Spaceflight Now and SpacePolicyOnline; VIPER, NASA.
